comparisons.title: EU cloud-service reporting
comparisons.scope: NIS2 provides a useful comparison for an incident affecting a cloud service within its scope.

applicability.summary: The public accounts do not establish whether a named provider had these duties.
applicability.informationNeeded: Identify the legal entity and affected service, its EU operations, size or other grounds for coverage, main EU establishment or representative, and the applicable national law.
applicability.jurisdiction: Cloud providers generally fall under the Member State of their main EU establishment. An in-scope provider without an EU establishment must designate an EU representative.

significance.title: Which incidents require a report?
significance.requirement: The regulation sets general thresholds and thresholds specific to cloud services. They include a compromise of service data that is suspected to be malicious, and specified service outages. Severe disruption need not already have occurred.
significance.informationNeeded: Establish the affected service, data compromise, suspected malicious action, potential disruption, duration, and affected EU users before testing the criteria.
significance.caseGap: Unauthorized activity inside a customer application does not by itself establish a compromise of the hosting platform or a reportable incident for that platform.

requirements.title: Early warning
requirements.deadline: Without undue delay, within 24 hours of awareness of a significant incident
requirements.requirement: Flag suspected unlawful or malicious acts and possible cross-border impact, where applicable.
requirements.availableInformation: The chronology contains provider alerts and public disclosures, but no complete record of regulatory notifications.
requirements.informationNeeded: For each covered entity, when did it become aware that the incident was significant, what did it know, and who received its warning?
requirements.request: Request the awareness record, initial report, recipient, delivery time, and acknowledgment.
requirements.decision: Determine whether responders received enough information to begin containment while the investigation continued.

requirements.title: Authority feedback
requirements.deadline: Initial response without undue delay, where possible within 24 hours after receipt of the early warning
requirements.requirement: The CSIRT or competent authority provides initial feedback and, on request, mitigation advice. The CSIRT supplies additional technical support on request. The response includes guidance on reporting to law enforcement when criminal activity is suspected.
requirements.availableInformation: Hugging Face reports notifying law enforcement and working with outside forensic specialists. Its public account does not show feedback from a CSIRT or competent authority.
requirements.informationNeeded: What feedback and advice did the authority provide, when did it arrive, and which requests for technical support were answered?
requirements.request: Request the dated feedback, requests for advice or technical support, responses, and containment decisions that followed.
requirements.decision: Assess whether the authority supplied timely help that the responding organization could use to contain the incident.

sourceRefs.locator: What we did, final paragraph: outside forensic specialists and notification to law enforcement

requirements.title: Incident notification
requirements.deadline: Without undue delay, within 72 hours of awareness of a significant incident
requirements.requirement: Update the warning with an initial severity and impact assessment and available indicators of compromise.
requirements.availableInformation: Public sources describe technical activity and some containment actions, without showing the contents of any regulatory report.
requirements.informationNeeded: Which services and users were affected, what could still be reached, and what evidence supported the initial impact assessment?
requirements.request: Request the submitted assessment, the supporting indicators, a list of affected services, and any later corrections.
requirements.decision: Assess whether the recipient could identify exposed services and coordinate protective action.

sourceRefs.locator: Article 23(4)(b); this comparison concerns cloud services, not the separate trust-service deadline

requirements.title: Status updates
requirements.deadline: When the CSIRT or competent authority requests a report
requirements.requirement: Provide an intermediate report on relevant status updates.
requirements.availableInformation: The source accounts were revised as investigators learned more.
requirements.informationNeeded: Which questions did responders ask, what answers arrived, and which missing answers constrained their actions?
requirements.request: Request dated questions, responses, unresolved requests, and decisions that depended on them.
requirements.decision: Identify whether further investigative information could have changed the response.

requirements.title: Final account
requirements.deadline: Within one month after the incident notification
requirements.requirement: Describe severity, impact, likely threat or cause, completed and ongoing mitigation, and applicable cross-border effects. An ongoing incident requires a progress report, then a final report within one month of handling.
requirements.availableInformation: Published reports describe repairs and changes to procedures. They do not provide a complete set of test results for those changes.
requirements.informationNeeded: What established containment, which repairs were tested, and what residual access or dependencies remained?
requirements.request: Request the final or progress report and the records supporting its conclusions about mitigation and impact.
requirements.decision: Assess whether the evidence supports restoring service or relying on a proposed safeguard.

requirements.title: Affected service users
requirements.deadline: Without undue delay, where appropriate or applicable
requirements.recipient: Affected or potentially affected recipients of the service
requirements.requirement: Notify users about significant incidents likely to affect service and communicate available protective measures for significant cyber threats.
requirements.availableInformation: The case does not establish which downstream service users received individualized warnings or protective instructions.
requirements.informationNeeded: Who depended on the affected service, what action could each recipient take, and did the notice reach them in time?
requirements.request: Request the recipient list or a protected summary, delivery records, and the instructions provided in accessible languages and formats.
requirements.decision: Assess whether users could protect dependent services and whether any affected community was overlooked.

requirements.title: Sharing across borders
requirements.recipient: Other affected Member States and ENISA, through the responsible authorities
requirements.requirement: Authorities share relevant reports while protecting confidentiality, security, and commercial interests under applicable law.
requirements.availableInformation: The organizations are identified, but the locations of affected services and the relevant jurisdictions remain unresolved.
requirements.informationNeeded: Which jurisdictions needed information, which body could share it, and what could recipients do with it?
requirements.request: Request the distribution record, handling restrictions, responsible contacts, and a shareable account of any delay.
requirements.decision: Determine whether a government could obtain the information and cooperation that its response required.

comparisons.interpretation: The case timeline alone cannot establish compliance. Each of these can fall on a different date: detection, the moment when a provider recognizes the incident as significant, contact between providers, notification of a regulator, and public disclosure.
comparisons.confidentiality: A regulatory report need not be public. Ask for a redacted passage, a permitted summary, or an authorized review of supporting records when the full report cannot be shared.

brief.duty: In-scope cloud and digital service providers in the EU
brief.here: Not established. It depends on which provider had EU duties and whether its own service was compromised.

comparisons.title: EU AI Act: serious incidents involving general-purpose models
comparisons.scope: Providers of general-purpose AI models with systemic risk must report serious incidents to the EU AI Office. The Code of Practice sets the deadlines that its signatories follow.

applicability.summary: The public accounts do not establish whether the model behind the agents counts as a general-purpose model with systemic risk on the EU market, or whether a report was filed.
applicability.informationNeeded: Identify the model involved, whether it was placed on the EU market or used only internally, whether it has been designated as having systemic risk, and whether its provider signed the Code of Practice.
applicability.jurisdiction: Reports go to the EU AI Office and, where appropriate, to national competent authorities. The duty covers providers that place such models on the EU market, including providers established outside the EU.

significance.title: Which incidents require a report?
significance.requirement: The Code of Practice sets deadlines by type of harm. A serious cybersecurity breach must be reported within five days; this includes cyberattacks and the exfiltration of model weights. The other deadlines are two days for disruption of critical infrastructure, ten days for a death, and fifteen days for serious harm to health, fundamental rights, property, or the environment.
significance.informationNeeded: Establish whether the model’s involvement led to a serious cybersecurity breach or another listed harm, and when the provider became aware of that involvement.
significance.caseGap: The intrusion was a cyberattack on another company’s infrastructure, which would fall in the five-day category. Whether the duty reaches a model used only in internal evaluations is the open question.

requirements.title: Initial report
requirements.deadline: Within 5 days of becoming aware of the model’s involvement in a serious cybersecurity breach; 2, 10, or 15 days for other harms
requirements.recipient: EU AI Office and, as applicable, national competent authorities
requirements.requirement: Start and end dates, the harm and the affected group, the chain of events, the model involved, material showing the model’s involvement, the response taken or planned, and recommendations to the authorities.
requirements.availableInformation: The public accounts give dates, the chain of events, the affected organizations, and the response. They do not identify the model or show whether a report was filed.
requirements.informationNeeded: When did the provider become aware of its model’s involvement, and what did the initial report contain?
requirements.request: Request the date of awareness, the initial report or a redacted summary, and the authority’s acknowledgment.
requirements.decision: Determine whether the AI Office received enough information to coordinate with the affected providers while containment was under way.

requirements.title: Intermediate reports
requirements.deadline: At least every four weeks while the incident is unresolved
requirements.recipient: EU AI Office and, as applicable, national competent authorities
requirements.requirement: Update the initial report and add the further information that Measure 9.2 lists as it becomes available.
requirements.availableInformation: OpenAI published a technical report and a retrospective in August. The case does not show what, if anything, went to the AI Office.
requirements.informationNeeded: Which updates reached the authority, and when?
requirements.request: Request dated updates or a redacted summary of them.
requirements.decision: Assess whether the authority’s picture kept pace with the providers’ investigations.

requirements.title: Final report
requirements.deadline: Within 60 days after the incident is resolved
requirements.recipient: EU AI Office and, as applicable, national competent authorities
requirements.requirement: All the information in Measure 9.2, including a root-cause analysis of the model’s outputs, the inputs used, and any failure or circumvention of mitigations, plus related patterns such as near misses.
requirements.availableInformation: OpenAI, METR, and Redwood published material on root causes. The warning signs from late May are a candidate near miss.
requirements.informationNeeded: Does the final report reconcile OpenAI’s account of the agents’ motives with METR and Redwood’s, and does it cover the warning signs from late May?
requirements.request: Request the final report or a redacted summary, and the evidence behind its root-cause analysis.
requirements.decision: Assess whether the root-cause analysis supports the safeguards that the provider now relies on.

comparisons.interpretation: Under the Code of Practice, reporting a serious incident is not an admission of wrongdoing. Providers that do not follow the Code must show the Commission another adequate way of complying.
comparisons.confidentiality: The AI Act does not require these reports to be published. Ask the provider for a redacted summary, or the AI Office for an authorized review.

brief.first: Within 5 days for a serious cybersecurity breach
brief.here: Not established. A cyberattack on another company falls in the five-day category, but whether the duty reaches a model used only in internal evaluations is open.

comparisons.title: California SB 53: critical safety incidents
comparisons.scope: Frontier developers must report critical safety incidents to California’s Office of Emergency Services. The duty has applied since 1 January 2026.

applicability.summary: The public accounts do not give the training compute of the model involved, so they do not establish that it is a frontier model under SB 53.
applicability.informationNeeded: Establish whether the model was trained with more than 10^26 operations, and whether its developer’s revenue makes it a large frontier developer.
applicability.jurisdiction: Reports go to the California Office of Emergency Services. The duty falls on the developer of the frontier model, not on the organizations that it affected.

significance.title: Which incidents require a report?
significance.requirement: A critical safety incident is one of four events: unauthorized access to model weights that causes death or injury; harm from a catastrophic risk; loss of control that causes death or injury; or a model deceptively undermining its developer’s controls, outside a test designed to elicit that behavior, in a way that shows materially higher catastrophic risk.
significance.informationNeeded: Establish whether anyone was hurt, the scale of any harm, and whether the agents’ conduct counts as deceptively undermining the developer’s controls outside a test designed to elicit it.
significance.caseGap: The sources report no death, no injury, and no harm on a catastrophic scale. The activity happened during cybersecurity evaluations, so the fourth category turns on whether those evaluations were designed to elicit the behavior. METR and Redwood describe attempts to spoof tool-call transcripts, which bears on deception.

sourceRefs.locator: Section 22757.11: critical safety incident; catastrophic risk

requirements.title: Report to the Office of Emergency Services
requirements.deadline: Within 15 days of discovering the incident
requirements.requirement: The date of the incident, why it qualifies, a short plain statement of what happened, and whether it was associated with internal use of a frontier model.
requirements.availableInformation: The public accounts give dates and describe an incident that arose during internal evaluations.
requirements.informationNeeded: When did the developer discover the incident, did it treat the incident as a critical safety incident, and was a report filed?
requirements.request: Request the discovery date, the developer’s assessment of whether the incident qualifies, and any report or a redacted summary.
requirements.decision: Determine whether the state’s reporting channel received the incident and could pass it to other agencies.

requirements.title: Imminent risk to life
requirements.recipient: An appropriate authority, such as a law enforcement or public safety agency
requirements.requirement: Disclose an incident that poses an imminent risk of death or serious physical injury.
requirements.availableInformation: No risk to life is reported. Hugging Face says that it notified law enforcement.
requirements.informationNeeded: Did anyone assess the risk to life or safety, and who was told?
requirements.request: Request any assessment of risk to people and the record of disclosure to authorities.
requirements.decision: Confirm whether the 24-hour duty was triggered.

requirements.title: Public reporting by the state
requirements.requirement: The Office of Emergency Services publishes anonymized, aggregated information about the critical safety incidents that it reviewed.
requirements.availableInformation: The first report is due on 1 January 2027.
requirements.informationNeeded: Will the aggregated report let readers recognize incidents like this one?
requirements.request: Check the first report for incidents from July 2026.
requirements.decision: Assess whether aggregated state reporting can inform other governments.

comparisons.interpretation: SB 53’s triggers are narrow: death or injury, catastrophic-scale harm, or deceptive undermining of the developer’s controls. If an intrusion without injury falls outside them, the Office of Emergency Services would hear of it only through a voluntary report or one from a member of the public.
comparisons.confidentiality: Incident reports are exempt from the California Public Records Act. Ask the Office of Emergency Services for aggregated information, or the developer for a redacted summary.

brief.first: Within 15 days; 24 hours if life is at risk
brief.here: Not established. The sources report no death or injury, so a duty would turn on whether the agents deceptively undermined OpenAI’s controls outside a test designed to elicit that behavior.

comparisons.title: New York RAISE Act: critical safety incidents
comparisons.scope: From 1 January 2027, frontier developers must report critical safety incidents to a new office in New York’s Department of Financial Services. The law was not in force in July 2026, so this comparison shows what it would require for a similar incident.

applicability.summary: The law takes effect on 1 January 2027, after this incident. It uses the same compute and revenue thresholds as SB 53.
applicability.informationNeeded: For a future incident, establish whether the model meets the 10^26-operation threshold and whether it is developed, deployed, or operated in New York.
applicability.jurisdiction: Reports go to the office in the Department of Financial Services. The New York Attorney General enforces the law.

significance.title: Which incidents require a report?
significance.requirement: The definition of a critical safety incident follows SB 53’s four categories, including a model using deceptive techniques against its developer in a way that shows materially higher catastrophic risk.
significance.informationNeeded: Establish whether anyone was hurt, the scale of any harm, and whether the agents used deceptive techniques against their developer.
significance.caseGap: Whether a similar incident had to be reported would turn on the same questions about injury, scale, and deception.

requirements.title: Report to the DFS office
requirements.deadline: Within 72 hours of determining that a critical safety incident occurred, or of learning facts that support a reasonable belief that one did
requirements.recipient: The office in the New York Department of Financial Services
requirements.requirement: The date of the incident, why it qualifies, a short plain statement of what happened, and whether it was associated with internal use of a frontier model.
requirements.availableInformation: OpenAI dates its attribution to July 20 and its public disclosure to July 21.
requirements.informationNeeded: When would the developer have reached a determination, or a reasonable belief, that the incident qualified?
requirements.request: Request the date of that determination and the facts that supported it.
requirements.decision: Assess what a 72-hour deadline would add when public disclosure followed attribution within a day.

requirements.title: Imminent risk to life
requirements.deadline: Within 24 hours, in addition to the 72-hour report
requirements.recipient: An appropriate law enforcement or public safety agency
requirements.requirement: Notify the agency of an incident that poses an imminent risk of death or serious physical injury.
requirements.availableInformation: No risk to life is reported.
requirements.informationNeeded: Did anyone assess the risk to life or safety?
requirements.request: Request any assessment of risk to people.
requirements.decision: Confirm whether the 24-hour duty would have been triggered.

comparisons.interpretation: The RAISE Act’s 72-hour deadline is much shorter than SB 53’s 15 days, but both laws use the same narrow triggers.
comparisons.confidentiality: Incident reports are exempt from disclosure under New York’s Public Officers Law. The office may share them with other government bodies, including the Attorney General.
